chunks: Ali narrated from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Muhammad ibn Aslam al-Jabali, from Ali ibn Abi Hamza, from Aban ibn Taghlib, who said:

I said to Abu Abdullah (peace be upon him), 'We travel and do not have bran with us, so we rub ourselves with fine flour.' He said, 'There is no problem. The spoilage is in what harms the body and wastes wealth. As for what improves the body, it is not spoilage. I sometimes order my slave to prepare for me pure flour with oil, so I rub myself with it.'

key_terms.الْفَسَاد: Spoilage or corruption (in the context of ritual purity/usage)
key_terms.نُخَالَة: Bran (husk of grain), traditionally used for rubbing the body

ai.seo_question: Is it permissible to use flour instead of bran for rubbing the body in Islamic jurisprudence?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) establishes a functional criterion for *fasad* (spoilage/waste) in personal hygiene, ruling that using fine flour for rubbing the body is permissible as long as it benefits the skin rather than causing harm or excessive financial loss. This hadith highlights the Shia juristic principle that utility and preservation of health can justify the use of otherwise valuable resources, a concept further illustrated by the Imam’s personal practice of using pure oil for this purpose. It reflects the broader Shia emphasis on practical ease (*rukhas*) in travel while maintaining standards of cleanliness and economic prudence.
